title: Client Credentials Flow
description: Implement machine-to-machine authentication using the OAuth2 Client Credentials grant type.

data.text: The Client Credentials flow is the simplest OAuth 2.0 flow and is used exclusively for machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication. There is no user involved — the client authenticates with its own credentials (client_id and client_secret) and receives a token representing the service itself. This token is then used to access APIs or other services on behalf of the client, not any particular user.

items: Backend services calling other backend services (e.g., a billing service calling a payment API)
Scheduled jobs or cron tasks that need API access
Microservices authenticating to an internal API gateway
CI/CD pipelines that need to authenticate to deployment APIs
Service accounts in Kubernetes or cloud environments

data.title: No user context
data.text: Tokens issued through Client Credentials represent the client itself, not a user. Any scopes in the token are limited to what the client is authorized to access. This means you cannot use this flow to access user-specific data — only service-level or client-level resources.

The client authenticates with the authorization server using its client credentials. The request is a POST to the token endpoint with grant_type=client_credentials. If valid, the server responds with an access token. The client then uses that token to call the protected API.

data.caption: Client Credentials flow — direct machine-to-machine token exchange
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant AuthServer
    participant ResourceServer
    Client->>AuthServer: POST /token (grant_type=client_credentials, client_id, client_secret, scope)
    AuthServer->>AuthServer: Validate client credentials
    AuthServer->>Client: access_token + expires_in
    Client->>ResourceServer: GET /api/resource (Authorization: Bearer access_token)
    ResourceServer->>Client: Protected resource

data.title: Token caching strategy
data.text: Client Credentials tokens are often used across many requests. Always cache the token and its expiry. Request a new token only when the cached one is about to expire — this reduces load on the authorization server and avoids rate limiting.

data.title: Scope validation is critical
data.text: The authorization server must validate that the requested scopes are within the client's allowed scope set. Never let a client request arbitrary scopes or escalate privileges. The token should carry only the minimum scopes needed for the intended operation.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Client Credentials is the only OAuth flow with no user involvement
Use it for service-to-service, scheduled jobs, and CI/CD pipelines
Always cache tokens and request new ones only near expiration
Validate scope — tokens carry only the client's allowed scopes
The issued token has no 'sub' (user subject) claim
Protect the client secret — rotate it regularly in production
data.takeaway: Client Credentials is the simplest OAuth flow, but it's only correct when no user identity is needed.
